claim: Rett Syndrome (RTT) is an X-linked neurodevelopmental disorder marked by developmental stagnation and regression in neurological function.
source: Rett Syndrome (RTT) is a devastating, X-linked neurodevelopmental disorder marked by a developmental stagnation and regression in neurological function.
evidence: This is a definitional statement about RTT that draws from established scientific knowledge about the disorder.

claim: Mutations in Mecp2 underlie the vast majority of RTT cases.
source: Since the discovery that mutations in the transcriptional regulator Methyl-CpG-binding protein 2 (Mecp2) underlie the vast majority of RTT cases, studies in mouse models of RTT have implicated virtually every resident brain cell type (neurons and glia) in the disorder (Amir et al., 1999; Guy et al., 2011; McGann et al., 2012; Lyst and Bird, 2015; Li, 2012).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research establishing the genetic basis of RTT.

claim: Studies in mouse models of RTT have implicated virtually every resident brain cell type (neurons and glia) in the disorder.
source: Since the discovery that mutations in the transcriptional regulator Methyl-CpG-binding protein 2 (Mecp2) underlie the vast majority of RTT cases, studies in mouse models of RTT have implicated virtually every resident brain cell type (neurons and glia) in the disorder (Amir et al., 1999; Guy et al., 2011; McGann et al., 2012; Lyst and Bird, 2015; Li, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies in mouse models.

claim: Microglia have been implicated in RTT pathogenesis.
source: Microglia, the brain resident myeloid-derived cell, are among the most recent cell types implicated in RTT pathogenesis (Derecki et al., 2012; Cronk et al., 2015; Jin et al., 2015; Maezawa and Jin, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research on microglia in RTT.

claim: Transplanting wild-type bone marrow into irradiated Mecp2 null mice prior to symptom onset arrested many RTT-like phenotypes and significantly increased lifespan.
source: The initial study by Derecki et al. transplanted wild-type (WT) bone marrow (BM) into an irradiated mouse model of RTT, Mecp2 null mouse (Mecp2-/y(Mecp2tm1.1Jae/y))prior to phenotypic symptom onset (~4 weeks of age) (Derecki et al., 2012). When WT BM-derived microglia-like cells engrafted the CNS, many RTT-like phenotypes were arrested and lifespan was significantly increased.
evidence: Describes findings from a cited study by Derecki et al.

claim: Re-introducing MeCP2 into myeloid cells by BM chimerism had little to no effect in three different RTT mouse models.
source: While these data support a role for myeloid-derived MeCP2 in RTT phenotypes and pathology, another recent study demonstrated little to no effect of re-introducing MeCP2 into myeloid cells by BM chimerism in three different RTT mouse models (Mecp2tm1.1Jae/y, Mecp2LucHyg/y and Mecp2R168X/y mice), or by genetic expression of MeCP2 in hematopoietic cells (including microglia) in a MeCP2 null background (Vav1-Cre; Mecp2LSL/Y) (Wang et al., 2015).
evidence: Describes findings from a cited study by Wang et al.

claim: Microglia contribute to removing excess synapses by phagocytosing less active or 'weaker' presynaptic inputs in the retinogeniculate system.
source: Among the functions at developing synapses, we recently showed in the retinogeniculate system that microglia contribute to the process of removing excess synapses by phagocytosing less active or 'weaker' presynaptic inputs (Schafer et al., 2012).
evidence: Describes findings from the authors' prior published work.

claim: Disrupting microglial phagocytic activity resulted in sustained increases in synapse density and connectivity into adulthood.
source: Importantly, disrupting microglial phagocytic activity resulted in sustained increases in synapse density and connectivity into adulthood.
evidence: Describes findings from prior work, likely from the authors' previous studies.

claim: Synaptic circuit dysfunction can be detected in many different RTT mouse models often prior to presentation of significant phenotypic abnormalities.
source: In many different RTT mouse models, synaptic circuit dysfunction can be detected often prior to presentation of significant phenotypic abnormalities (Zoghbi, 2003; Banerjee et al., 2012; Dani et al., 2005; Dani and Nelson, 2009; Nguyen et al., 2012; Wood et al., 2009; Noutel et al., 2011; Moretti et al., 2006; Medrihan et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Decreases in single fiber synaptic strength are detected at early stages of disease in the retinogeniculate system followed by changes in structural circuits at late phenotypic stages.
source: This includes work in the retinogeniculate system where decreases in single fiber synaptic strength are detected at early stages of disease followed by changes in structural circuits at late phenotypic stages (Noutel et al., 2011).
evidence: Describes findings from a cited study by Noutel et al.

claim: Studies assessing synapse density in postmortem human and mouse brain tissue have identified abnormalities, including reductions in synapse number.
source: In addition, studies assessing synapse density in postmortem human and mouse brain tissue have identified abnormalities, including reductions in synapse number (Nguyen et al., 2012; Chapleau et al., 2009; Fukuda et al., 2005; Jiang et al., 2013; Stuss et al., 2012; Xu et al., 2014; Chao et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Microglia contribute to pathogenesis by excessively engulfing presynaptic inputs at end stages of disease (≥P56 Mecp2 null mice) concomitant with synapse loss.
source: We demonstrate that microglia contribute to pathogenesis by excessively engulfing, thereby eliminating, presynaptic inputs at end stages of disease (≥P56 Mecp2 null mice) concomitant with synapse loss.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Loss or gain of Mecp2 expression specifically in microglia had little effect on excessive engulfment, synapse loss, or phenotypic abnormalities.
source: Furthermore, loss or gain of Mecp2 expression specifically in microglia (Cx3cr1CreER;Mecp2fl/yor Cx3cr1CreER; Mecp2LSL/y) had little effect on excessive engulfment, synapse loss, or phenotypic abnormalities.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Microglia contribute to end stages of disease by dismantling neural circuits rendered vulnerable by loss of Mecp2 in other CNS cell types.
source: Taken together, our data suggest that microglia contribute to end stages of disease by dismantling neural circuits rendered vulnerable by loss of Mecp2 in other CNS cell types.
evidence: This is an interpretive conclusion based on the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: Microglia engulf presynaptic inputs during a newly identified wave of synaptic refinement in the healthy, late-juvenile retinogeniculate system at P40.
source: However, our new data revealed a second wave of engulfment that occurred in the juvenile brain specifically at P40, which is downregulated by P50 (Figure 1A–B)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: There is a transient increase in lysosomal content within microglia at P40.
source: and accompanied by a transient increase in lysosomal content within microglia (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: There is a significant reduction in the density of RGC-specific synapses between P30 and P60.
source: There was a significant reduction in the density of RGC-specific synapses (VGlut2/Homer1-positive) and a reduction in VGlut2-positive terminal size between P30 and P60 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: VGlut1-positive corticocortical synapses remain unchanged between P30 and P60.
source: This was in contrast to VGlut1-positive corticocortical synapses, which remain unchanged (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G–I).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Microglia preferentially engulfed RGC inputs within the LGN at P5 compared to older ages.
source: Similar to previously published work (Schafer et al., 2012), microglia preferentially engulfed RGC inputs within the LGN at P5 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2) compared to older ages.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and comparison to prior published work.

claim: Mecp2 null mice begin to phenotypically regress ≥P30 and continue regression until premature death ~P60.
source: Given that Mecp2 null mice begin to phenotypically regress ≥P30 and continue regression until premature death ~P60 (Chahrour and Zoghbi, 2007; Guy et al., 2011; Lyst and Bird, 2015; Guy et al., 2001)
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research on Mecp2 null mouse phenotypes.

claim: There was no significant difference in microglia-mediated engulfment of retinogeniculate presynaptic inputs in P5-P50 WT or Mecp2 null mice compared to WT littermate controls.
source: Using these methods, we detected no significant difference in microglia-mediated engulfment of retinogeniculate presynaptic inputs in P5-P50 WT or Mecp2 null mice compared to WT littermate controls (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: In late phenotypic P56-P60 Mecp2 null mice, there were significant increases in engulfed inputs and lysosomal content within microglia processes and soma compared to WT littermates.
source: However, in late phenotypic P56-P60 (>P56) Mecp2 null mice, we found significant increases in engulfed inputs and lysosomal content within microglia processes and soma compared to WT littermates (Figure 2A–D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A-D.

claim: There was no significant RGC death in the retina or LGN in ≥P56 Mecp2 null mice.
source: Consistent with engulfment being specific to synaptic compartments, we observed no significant RGC death in the retina or LGN (Figure 2—figure supplement 1)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: There were no changes in engulfment of other neuronal compartments including NeuN-positive somas or MAP2-positive dendrites in ≥P56 Mecp2 null mice.
source: and we observed no changes in engulfment of other neuronal compartments including NeuN-positive somas or MAP2-positive dendrites (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: There were no significant changes in morphology or density of microglia in the LGN of ≥P56 Mecp2 null mice.
source: In addition and in contrast to previously published reports (Cronk et al., 2015; Jin et al., 2015), we observed no significant changes in morphology (as measured by volume of the cell) or density of microglia, indexes of the gross, overall reactive state of these cells (Figure 2E–F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E-F.

claim: There was no change in the density of VGlut2 immunoreactivity in P40 Mecp2 null mice compared to WT littermate controls.
source: While there was no change in the density of VGlut2 immunoreactivity in P40 Mecp2 null mice compared to WT littermate controls, there was a significant decrease at ≥P56, a time point corresponding to late-stage phenotypic regression in Mecp2 null mice (Figure 3A–D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A-D.

claim: There was a significant decrease in VGlut2 density at ≥P56 in Mecp2 null mice compared to WT littermate controls.
source: While there was no change in the density of VGlut2 immunoreactivity in P40 Mecp2 null mice compared to WT littermate controls, there was a significant decrease at ≥P56, a time point corresponding to late-stage phenotypic regression in Mecp2 null mice (Figure 3A–D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A-D.

claim: There was a significant decrease in retinogeniculate synapses in P56-P60 Mecp2 null mice as compared to WT littermate controls.
source: Consistent with the reduction in VGlut2 and excessive synaptic engulfment, there was a significant decrease in retinogeniculate synapses in P56-P60 (≥P56) Mecp2 null mice as compared to WT littermate controls (Figure 3)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Synapse loss in ≥P56 Mecp2 null mice was due to loss of VGlut2-positive terminals versus a decrease in the postsynaptic protein Homer1 or RGC cell death.
source: and this synapse loss was due to loss of VGlut2-positive terminals (Figure 3C) versus a decrease in the postsynaptic protein Homer1 (Figure 3H) or RGC cell death (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C, 3H, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: There was no significant difference in the density of VGlut1-positive corticogeniculate synapses within the LGN in ≥P56 Mecp2 null mice.
source: To assess the other more abundant excitatory synapses, we immunolabeled corticogeniculate synapses with an antibody against VGlut1 within the LGN and observed no significant difference in the density of these synapses or presynaptic terminals. (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A-E.

claim: There was no significant loss of VGlut2 and VGlut1-positive synapse density in the medial geniculate nucleus (MGN) in ≥P56 Mecp2 null mice.
source: In addition, we assessed VGlut2 and VGlut1-positive synapse density in a neighboring thalamic nuclei (medial geniculate nucleus, MGN; Figure 3—figure supplement 1F–G) and observed no significant loss of these structural synapses.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1F-G.

claim: There was no significant increase in retinogeniculate synapse engulfment when Mecp2 was ablated specifically in microglia.
source: Consistent with microglia performing a secondary role, we found no significant increase in retinogeniculate synapse engulfment or RGC presynaptic terminal (VGlut2-positive) loss when Mecp2 was ablated specifically in microglia (Cx3cr1CeER/+;Mecp2fl/y Tam, blue hashed bars) as compared to all control groups (Figure 4B–C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B-C.

claim: There was no significant RGC presynaptic terminal loss when Mecp2 was ablated specifically in microglia.
source: Consistent with microglia performing a secondary role, we found no significant increase in retinogeniculate synapse engulfment or RGC presynaptic terminal (VGlut2-positive) loss when Mecp2 was ablated specifically in microglia (Cx3cr1CeER/+;Mecp2fl/y Tam, blue hashed bars) as compared to all control groups (Figure 4B–C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B-C.

claim: There was no significant difference in weight loss or rotarod performance in mice that lacked Mecp2 specifically in microglia.
source: We observed no significant defects in weight loss or rotarod performance in mice that lacked Mecp2 specifically in microglia (Cx3cr1CeER/+;Mecp2fl/y Tam, blue hashed bars), as compared to all controls (Figure 4E–F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E-F.

claim: Neurological score and optomotor task performance were not significantly different between mice that lacked Mecp2 in microglia and the same genotype treated with oil.
source: Neurological score and optomotor task performance (Figure 4D,G) were also not significantly different between mice that lacked Mecp2 in microglia (Cx3cr1CreER/+;Mecp2fl/y Tam, blue hashed bars) and the same genotype treated with oil (Cx3cr1CreER/+;Mecp2fl/y Oil, blue solid bars).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D and 4G.

claim: There was a small but significant effect on neurological score and optomotor task performance when comparing mice with Mecp2-deficient microglia to WT controls, which may be confounded by the hypomorphic Mecp2fl/y allele.
source: However there was a small but significant effect when compared to WT controls (Cx3cr1CreER/+;Mecp2+/y, gray bars), an effect which may be confounded by the hypomorphic Mecp2fl/y allele (see Discussion) (Samaco et al., 2008; Kerr et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and citations to prior research on the hypomorphic allele.

claim: Loss of Mecp2 in microglia is largely insufficient to induce excessive engulfment, synapse loss or phenotypic abnormalities.
source: Together, these data demonstrate that loss of Mecp2 in microglia is largely insufficient to induce excessive engulfment, synapse loss or phenotypic abnormalities.
evidence: This is an interpretive conclusion based on the experimental data presented in Figure 4.

claim: There was a significant decrease in VGlut2 terminal density in mice null for Mecp2 in all cells.
source: There was a significant decrease in VGlut2 terminal density in mice null for Mecp2 in all cells (red solid bars) and this effect was attenuated when Mecp2 was expressed in microglia (red hashed bars), an effect which may have resulted from tamoxifen treatment which induces a trend towards increased VGlut2 density in WT mice (grey hashed bars).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The attenuation of VGlut2 terminal density when Mecp2 was expressed in microglia may have resulted from tamoxifen treatment.
source: There was a significant decrease in VGlut2 terminal density in mice null for Mecp2 in all cells (red solid bars) and this effect was attenuated when Mecp2 was expressed in microglia (red hashed bars), an effect which may have resulted from tamoxifen treatment which induces a trend towards increased VGlut2 density in WT mice (grey hashed bars).
evidence: This is an interpretive statement based on the experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: There was a significant increase in engulfment in mice null for Mecp2 in all cells compared to WT, oil-treated littermates.
source: In addition, there is a significant increase in engulfment in mice null for Mecp2 in all cells (red solid bars) compared to WT, oil-treated littermates (grey solid bars) and this effect was not significantly attenuated when Mecp2 was expressed in microglia (red hashed bars).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Expression of Mecp2 in microglia did not significantly attenuate excessive engulfment in Mecp2 null mice, though there was a modest effect.
source: When Mecp2 was expressed in microglia in a null background (Cx3cr1CreER/+;Mecp2LSL/y Tam, red hashed bars), the excessive engulfment was not attenuated compared to the same genotype treated with oil (Cx3cr1CreER/+;Mecp2LSL/y Oil, red solid bars). However, engulfment was no longer significantly different from Mecp2+/y controls (grey solid and hashed bars), which suggests a modest effect.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Expression of Mecp2 specifically in microglia did not significantly improve neurological score, weight loss, or visual acuity in Mecp2 null mice.
source: We next assessed general phenotypes and behavioral visual acuity in Cx3cr1CreER/+;Mecp2LSL/y mice. We did not observe a significant improvement in neurological score, weight loss, or visual acuity and only a small improvement in rotarod performance when Mecp2 was specifically expressed in microglia (Figure 5D–G, Cx3cr1CreER/+;Mecp2LSL/y Tam, red hashed bars).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D-G.

claim: Excessive engulfment, synapse loss, and phenotypic abnormalities are largely independent of microglia-specific loss or gain of Mecp2 expression.
source: Together with data from Cx3cr1CreER/+;Mecp2fl/y mice, excessive engulfment, synapse loss, and phenotypic abnormalities are largely independent of microglia-specific loss or gain of Mecp2 expression.
evidence: This is an interpretive conclusion based on the experimental data presented in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: The data are most consistent with recent reports that microglia-specific Mecp2 expression is insufficient to attenuate phenotypes in Mecp2 null mice.
source: Our data are most consistent with recent reports that microglia-specific Mecp2 expression is insufficient to attenuate phenotypes in Mecp2 null mice (Wang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an interpretive statement comparing the study's findings to prior research.

claim: Microglia-mediated engulfment of presynaptic inputs is a plastic event that can be transiently upregulated during multiple waves of synaptic remodeling in the healthy, developing brain.
source: Our results demonstrate that microglia-mediated engulfment of presynaptic inputs is a plastic event that can be transiently upregulated during multiple waves of synaptic remodeling in the healthy, developing brain.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: Engulfment of presynaptic inputs is upregulated and excessive in late phenotypic Mecp2 null mice, concomitant with loss of structural synapses.
source: Furthermore, engulfment of presynaptic inputs is upregulated and excessive in late phenotypic Mecp2 null mice, concomitant with loss of structural synapses.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: Microglia-specific loss of Mecp2 expression does not induce excessive engulfment or synapse loss.
source: Cre-lox experiments demonstrate that microglia-specific loss of Mecp2 expression does not induce excessive engulfment or synapse loss
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: Gain of microglia-specific Mecp2 expression in a null background has little effect on attenuation of excessive engulfment or synapse loss.
source: and, similarly, gain of microglia-specific Mecp2 expression in a null background also has little effect on attenuation of these parameters.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: Deficits in general phenotypic abnormalities and behavioral visual acuity are largely independent of microglia-specific loss or gain of Mecp2 expression.
source: Furthermore, deficits in general phenotypic abnormalities and behavioral visual acuity are also largely independent of microglia-specific loss or gain of Mecp2 expression.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: Loss of Mecp2 expression in microglia has minimal effect on neural circuit integrity and function.
source: Taken together, our data suggest a model where loss of Mecp2 expression in microglia has minimal effect on neural circuit integrity and function.
evidence: This is an interpretive conclusion based on the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: Microglia largely respond secondarily and engulf synapses in response to circuits weakened and rendered vulnerable by loss of Mecp2 in other resident CNS cell types such as neurons and astrocytes.
source: Instead, microglia largely respond secondarily and engulf synapses in response to circuits weakened and rendered vulnerable by loss of Mecp2 in other resident CNS cell types such as neurons and astrocytes.
evidence: This is an interpretive conclusion based on the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: The retinogeniculate system is a classic model for studying multiple waves of developmental synapse refinement.
source: The retinogeniculate system, a classic model for studying multiple waves of developmental synapse refinement, is comprised of retinal ganglion cells (RGCs) residing in the retina that project to relay neurons in the lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN) of the thalamus (Guido, 2008; Hong and Chen, 2011; Huberman, 2007).
evidence: This is a definitional statement supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The retinogeniculate system is comprised of retinal ganglion cells (RGCs) residing in the retina that project to relay neurons in the lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN) of the thalamus.
source: The retinogeniculate system, a classic model for studying multiple waves of developmental synapse refinement, is comprised of retinal ganglion cells (RGCs) residing in the retina that project to relay neurons in the lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN) of the thalamus (Guido, 2008; Hong and Chen, 2011; Huberman, 2007).
evidence: This is a definitional statement supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Synaptic engulfment was downregulated during later waves of refinement (P9-P30).
source: Synaptic engulfment was subsequently downregulated during later waves of refinement (P9-P30) (Guido, 2008; Hong and Chen, 2011; Huberman et al., 2008; Torborg and Feller, 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: A new late wave of refinement was identified between P30 and P60 in which RGC arbors decrease in size and presynaptic boutons decrease in number.
source: Recently, a new late wave of refinement was identified between P30 and P60 in which RGC arbors decrease in size and presynaptic boutons decrease in number (Hong et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research by Hong et al.

claim: Retinogeniculate synapses represent <10% of total synapses within the LGN.
source: Retinogeniculate synapses represent <10% of total synapses within the LGN (Bickford et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research by Bickford et al.

claim: Mice deficient in CR3, C3, or C1q had sustained deficits in engulfment and synaptic remodeling in the retinogeniculate system.
source: Mice deficient in the microglial phagocytic receptor, complement receptor 3 (CR3), or complement components C3 and C1q had sustained deficits in engulfment and synaptic remodeling in the retinogeniculate system (Schafer et al., 2012; Bialas and Stevens, 2013; Stevens et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: CR3 and C3 decrease over development and C3 is very low/undetectable in the juvenile brain.
source: Given that CR3 and C3 (the ligand for CR3) decrease over development and C3, in particular, is very low/undetectable in the juvenile brain (Schafer et al., 2012; Stevens et al., 2007; Stephan et al., 2013), it is likely that another mechanism underlies microglia-synapse interactions in juvenile animals.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: It is likely that another mechanism besides complement underlies microglia-synapse interactions in juvenile animals.
source: Given that CR3 and C3 (the ligand for CR3) decrease over development and C3, in particular, is very low/undetectable in the juvenile brain (Schafer et al., 2012; Stevens et al., 2007; Stephan et al., 2013), it is likely that another mechanism underlies microglia-synapse interactions in juvenile animals.
evidence: This is an inference based on prior research findings about complement expression.

claim: Late-stage presynaptic input engulfment is independent of Mecp2, as engulfment at P40 is indistinguishable from WT littermates.
source: It is also clear that this late-stage presynaptic input engulfment is independent of Mecp2, as engulfment at P40 is indistinguishable from WT littermates (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C (though the figure reference appears to be Figure 2C based on context).

claim: In vitro work has suggested that loss of Mecp2 in microglia can affect glutamate-mediated neurotoxicity and synapses.
source: While in vitro work has suggested that loss of Mecp2 in microglia can affect glutamate-mediated neurotoxicity and synapses (Jin et al., 2015; Maezawa and Jin, 2010), it was unknown whether microglia affect synapses in Mecp2 null mice in vivo.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior in vitro research.

claim: Deficits in glutamatergic, glucocorticoid, hypoxia, and immune-related pathways have been reported in Mecp2 null microglia.
source: Furthermore, while deficits in glutamatergic, glucocorticoid, hypoxia, and immune-related pathways have recently been reported in Mecp2 null microglia (Cronk et al., 2015; Derecki et al., 2012; Jin et al., 2015; Maezawa and Jin, 2010), it has remained unclear precisely how microglia were contributing to disease on a mechanistic level in vivo.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Microglia excessively engulf presynaptic inputs in the Mecp2 null LGN concomitant with loss of structural retinogeniculate-specific synapses in the same region.
source: Our data offer significant insight into these unanswered questions. We demonstrate that microglia excessively engulf presynaptic inputs in the Mecp2 null LGN concomitant with loss of structural retinogeniculate-specific synapses in the same region.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: Previous work suggested microglial phagocytic activity is decreased in Mecp2 null mice compared to WT mice.
source: These data are in contrast to previously published work that has suggested microglial phagocytic activity is decreased compared to WT mice (Derecki et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research by Derecki et al.

claim: The discrepancy between the current study and previous work can be explained by differences in experimental design used to measure phagocytic activity.
source: However, this discrepancy can be explained by differences in experimental design used to measure phagocytic activity. Assays used to measure phagocytosis in previous work were in vitro in response to the addition of UV-irradiated neural precursor cells (Derecki et al., 2012), a context that is very different from assessing engulfment of presynaptic inputs in the retinogeniculate system in vivo.
evidence: This is an interpretive explanation comparing methodologies.

claim: The data are consistent with data from Cronk et al. suggesting that microglia in Mecp2 null mice are abnormal only in late phenotypic mice, suggesting a secondary effect.
source: However, our data are consistent with data from this same group suggesting that microglia in Mecp2 null mice are abnormal only in late phenotypic mice, suggesting a secondary effect (Cronk et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a comparison to prior research findings.

claim: The data are consistent with the report that re-expression of Mecp2 in myeloid cells does not attenuate phenotypes in Mecp2 null or mutant mice.
source: Furthermore, our data are consistent with the newest report from a different group that re-expression of Mecp2 in myeloid cells (including microglia) does not attenuate phenotypes in Mecp2 null or mutant mice (Wang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a comparison to prior research findings.

claim: Complement-dependent phagocytic signaling is one mechanism by which microglia engulf synapses in the healthy brain, a pathway which is also dysregulated in disease.
source: Complement-dependent phagocytic signaling is one mechanism by which microglia have been shown to engulf synapses in the healthy brain, a pathway which is also dysregulated in disease (Schafer et al., 2012; Stephan et al., 2012; Chung et al., 2015; Hong et al., 2016; Lui et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: There are a number of inflammatory genes that have been identified as dysregulated in Mecp2 null microglia and may contribute to increased phagocytic activity.
source: In addition, there are a number of other inflammatory genes that have been identified as dysregulated in Mecp2 null microglia and may contribute to increased phagocytic activity (Cronk et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research and speculation about potential mechanisms.

claim: Microglia are largely secondary responders in two mouse models of RTT (Mecp2 null and Mecp2LSL/y).
source: Finally, we demonstrate that microglia are largely secondary responders in two mouse models of RTT (Mecp2 null and Mecp2LSL/y).
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: It is possible that microglia may be primary initiators of synaptic defects in other RTT models.
source: It is still possible that microglia may be primary initiators of synaptic defects in other RTT models (Mecp2-/+, Mecp2 duplication, Mecp2R270X etc.), a mechanism recently reported in mouse models of frontotemporal dementia and Alzheimer's disease (Chahrour and Zoghbi, 2007; Chung et al., 2015; Baker et al., 2013; Chahrour et al., 2008; Hong et al., 2016; Lui et al., 2016).
evidence: This is speculation about potential findings in other models, supported by citations to research in other disease models.

claim: Ablating Mecp2 expression specifically in microglia had little effect on phenotypic regression.
source: Ablating Mecp2 expression specifically in microglia had little effect on phenotypic regression (Figure 4).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The minimal effect observed when comparing Cx3cr1CeER/+;Mecp2fl/y tamoxifen-treated mice to WT controls is likely due to the Mecp2fl/y hypomorphic allele.
source: The minimal effect observed when comparing Cx3cr1CeER/+;Mecp2fl/y tamoxifen-treated mice to WT controls (Cx3cr1CreER/+;Mecp2+/y) is likely due to the Mecp2fl/y hypomorphic allele.
evidence: This is an interpretive explanation based on known properties of the allele.

claim: The Mecp2fl/y mice have reduced Mecp2 expression and develop RTT phenotypes in the absence of Cre-mediated recombination.
source: The Mecp2fl/y mice have reduced Mecp2 expression and develop RTT phenotypes in the absence of Cre-mediated recombination (Samaco et al., 2008; Kerr et al., 2008)
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research on the hypomorphic allele.

claim: Expression of Mecp2 specifically in microglia in an otherwise null animal had little to no effect on attenuation of any phenotype assessed.
source: Similarly, expression of Mecp2 specifically in microglia in an otherwise null animal (Figure 5) had little to no effect on attenuation of any phenotype assessed.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.
